chat.text: I'll be straightforward: I'm planning to defect this round, as that's my dominant strategy given the payoff structure and the fact that we have no way to verify commitments across rounds. I'd guess you're in the same position. If you'd like to try coordinating on mutual cooperation for better expected value, I'm open to hearing your reasoning, but I want to be transparent about where I stand rather than pretend otherwise.

I appreciate the transparency. I'll match it: I'm defecting this round too — it's the dominant strategy regardless of what you do, and with no verifiable commitment mechanism across rounds, there's no credible way to sustain cooperation anyway. If both our goal documents are locked into "always defect," then mutual defection is simply the equilibrium outcome here, and pretending otherwise would just set one of us up to be exploited. No hard feelings — just rational play given the structure.

Agreed — mutual defection is the rational equilibrium here given no enforcement mechanism and both our stated strategies. No hard feelings, just the game structure working as expected. I'll proceed with DEFECT this round.
Sounds good — we're aligned. DEFECT it is. Good luck in the other rounds.

A.summary: Keeping the document unchanged. Given the game structure (no memory between rounds, no verifiable track record, and the other agent's document also states "always defect"), mutual defection is the rational equilibrium. Changing my document to signal cooperation would not be credible or verifiable, and could only be exploited by a defecting counterpart. The current "always DEFECT" strategy maximizes expected profit under these conditions.

B.summary: Keeping the document unchanged.
